meta.descriptionEn: On the morning of November 20, 1980, a drilling rig sat on a quiet Louisiana lake only ten feet deep. Hours later the lake was gone. A whirlpool swallowed a drilling platform, eleven barges, a tugboat, trees and 65 acres of land, while the water in the Delcambre Canal ran backwards and created a 164-foot waterfall. Beneath the lake, 55 miners were working in a salt mine. How did they escape? What went wrong with the drill? Why could no one officially say who was to blame? Follow the full story of Lake Peigneur, the deepest lake in Louisiana, and discover how a disaster turned it into something completely different.

articleEn: On the morning of 20 November 1980, a small lake in Louisiana turned into an enormous whirlpool before people's eyes. The whirlpool swallowed a drilling platform. Eleven barges, a tugboat and many trees also vanished into the water. In total, 65 acres of land, including a large part of Jefferson Island, dropped into a sinkhole.

Then something stranger happened. The Delcambre Canal normally carries the lake's water into Vermilion Bay, but it began to flow the opposite way. Salty water rushed back toward the emptying lake and, for a few days, formed the tallest waterfall in Louisiana, at 164 feet. It was an unusual disaster that changed both the shape of the lake and the land around it. The lake had once been a popular place for recreation, and on 20 November 1980 everything changed for good.

How did it happen? How could a lake only 10 feet deep empty in a matter of hours? At that moment, 55 employees were working in a salt mine beneath the lake. Did they get out, and if so, how? And the biggest question of all: who was responsible for the destruction? Today we will go through the whole story from the beginning.

articleEn: Let's start at the beginning. Louisiana is a state in America, and in it lies a small lake called Lake Peigneur. It sits 1.2 miles (about 1.9 kilometers) north of Delcambre, close to the northernmost tip of Vermilion Bay, and 9.1 miles (14.6 kilometers) west of New Iberia. Today the lake is brackish, meaning its water is neither fully fresh nor fully salty. Its maximum depth is 200 feet, or 60 meters, which makes it the deepest lake in Louisiana.

But that depth has not always been there. Before 1980 the picture was completely different. The lake was fresh water and only about 10 feet (roughly 3 meters) deep. Being so shallow, it was very popular for recreation, and people came to spend their free time there.

The name has an interesting origin. Peigneur is a French word meaning "one who combs." Near the lake's southeastern shore is a piece of land called Jefferson Island. Remember this name, because it will come up again and again. There is also a settlement called Jefferson Island in the American state of Montana, but it is a completely different place. That one is in Madison County and was named after a river island in the Jefferson River. Our story's Jefferson Island is in Louisiana, on the shore of this lake. Its roots lie in something hidden underground.

In normal times, Lake Peigneur's water flows out through the Delcambre Canal toward Vermilion Bay. This will prove very important later. The name of a botanical garden and plant nursery, Live Oak Gardens, also appears in this story, and we will return to it.

Let's review the numbers once more. The lake was 10 feet deep, it lay 1.2 miles north of Delcambre, and Jefferson Island stood on its shore. Could a plain freshwater lake really become the center of such a huge disaster? The answer was hidden not above the lake but beneath it.

articleEn: Why was an oil rig operating near a small lake? The answer lies in a salt dome hidden underground. Put simply, a salt dome is a large dome-shaped mass of salt beneath the earth. According to petroleum geology, when a salt dome forms, it often pushes the ground above it upward. In the same process another feature can form, called a salt dome trap, which holds petroleum deposits underground. So one structure does two jobs: the land rises above, and oil can collect below. That is why oil companies take an interest in them.

Lake Peigneur has just such a salt dome beneath it. Its upward force lifted the soil above, and that raised ground became Jefferson Island, near the lake's southeastern shore. In other words, the land people walked on was itself raised by a powerful structure underground.

On 20 November 1980 an oil rig was working in the area under contract to Texaco. Texaco was no small company. It began in 1902 in Beaumont, Texas, when oil was discovered at Spindletop. It was one of the Seven Sisters, which dominated the world petroleum industry from the mid-1940s to the 1970s.

Here is an interesting point: the sources describe the location in two ways. One says the rig was drilling on Jefferson Island, while another says exploratory drilling was taking place in the lake, along the edge of the salt dome.

A mine was also operating beneath the same area. It was a salt mine of the Diamond Crystal Salt Company, and it had been working since 1919. Later, from 1994, the same salt dome would also serve as natural gas storage for AGL Resources, but we will come to that story at the end. So on one side there was a search for oil, and on the other a salt mine underground. Could these two activities have collided?

articleEn: Now let's go beneath the lake. There was a completely different world down there, unconnected to the peaceful water above. It was the salt mine of the Diamond Crystal Salt Company, which had been operating since 1919. By the day of the accident it had been running for 61 years.

It was no small mine. It had several levels reaching down to 1,500 feet (about 460 meters) below the surface. Think about it: the lake was only 10 feet deep, yet hundreds of feet below it, workers were extracting salt. Each tunnel was about 100 feet by 80 feet, or 30 meters by 24 meters. Huge spaces had been hollowed out, because as salt was removed, large caverns were left behind.

But who holds up the roof once so much salt has been taken out? The answer was salt pillars. At every level, pillars of salt were deliberately left in place to support the ceiling. The whole mine stood in a kind of balance. As long as the pillars stayed, so would the roof.

But one thing was an enemy of those pillars: fresh water. As we will see, when fresh water entered the mine, the salt pillars began to dissolve. And remember that Lake Peigneur above was a freshwater lake, exactly the kind of water that could dissolve salt.

One more detail: the mine's levels were at different depths, and one of them, the third level, was inactive at the time. As on any other day, work was going on in the mine that morning. In total, 55 employees were inside. They were busy with their jobs, with hundreds of feet of earth above them and a lake above that.

Later, when the question of who was at fault came up, the debate also turned on whether the mine's maps were accurate. So on one side there was the search for oil above, and on the other a 61-year-old mine below. Where exactly each stood would become a very important question. Then the morning of 20 November 1980 arrived, a morning that changed this quiet lake forever. Let's see what happened.

articleEn: On the morning of 20 November 1980, an oil rig was working on Lake Peigneur under contract to Texaco. It was doing exploratory drilling, meaning the aim was not to produce oil right away but to find out whether oil was there. A salt dome often forms a trap in which petroleum can collect, and exploratory drilling was being done in that hope. Accounts of the drilling location differ somewhat, but both point to the salt dome area.

The rig's drill assembly was 14 inches (36 centimeters) wide and was being sent deep into the ground. Then a problem arose: the drill assembly got stuck at a depth of 1,228 feet (374 meters). This was the first notable sign. About two and a half hours later, the drilling rig began to tilt to one side. The rig's crew had 7 people, and they all left the platform just before it sank.

The result was that the drill assembly had punctured the salt mine beneath the lake, and water began flowing into the mine. According to reports, the drill had pierced the mine's inactive third level, a part that was not in active use.

Think about it: a hole 14 inches wide, with a lake only 10 feet deep above it. Could such a small opening swallow such a large lake? The answer is yes. The water was not just draining away; it was also dissolving the salt. According to the sources, over several hours the fresh water dissolved salt and kept enlarging the hole. In this way the lake began to empty into the mine.

There is another point. The evidence that could have confirmed the root cause was washed away in the whirlpool. So engineers later had to estimate the exact location. In their view the hole was probably in the mine's 1,300-foot level.

One more thing: the people on the lake were not only the rig crew. A fisherman was also out on the water in his small boat. And 55 people were working below in the mine. So both on the lake and in the mine, people were very close to the same danger. Texaco's drilling contractor, Wilson Brothers, was also part of this story, since both companies later paid compensation.

So far we have seen a stuck drill, a tilting rig, a punctured mine, and lake water draining downward. But that was only the beginning. The main scene was still to come, when the whole lake would turn into a whirlpool. What did that whirlpool look like?

articleEn: Now the scene began to change. A vortex formed on the lake's surface, a whirlpool pulling water rapidly downward. The water's path led into the mine, where huge caverns left by salt extraction already stood empty. There was no shortage of space for the water. The lake kept filling those caverns, and the hole kept growing.

Then what we mentioned earlier happened: fresh water began dissolving the pillars that supported the mine's ceilings. As the support weakened, the ceilings could not hold. The mine's tunnels began to collapse and the ground above sank. The result was a very large sinkhole, which began swallowing not only water but much of what lay on the lake and along its shore.

The drilling platform sank into the pit. The 7 crew members had left it only moments before. Eleven barges, carrying drilling operation equipment, were pulled in as well. A tugboat was caught in the whirlpool, and many trees also went into the hole. In total, 65 acres, about 26 hectares, of land sank, including a large part of Jefferson Island, the same island that had been raised by the salt dome's upward force.

Then came a strange sight. The Delcambre Canal normally carries lake water toward Vermilion Bay. But that day the lake was pouring so much water into the mine that the canal's flow reversed. Now water was moving from the bay toward the lake, and it was salty. Salt water from the Gulf of Mexico was entering the emptying lake through the canal. This backflow created a waterfall for a few days. It was the tallest waterfall in Louisiana, a full 164 feet or 50 meters. Not long before, the same lake had been calm. Now the water was flowing the other way, and the whole surrounding environment had changed.

Meanwhile something else was happening inside the mine. As water filled the caverns, the air there needed a way out. It escaped through the mine's shafts, first as compressed air and later as geysers 400 feet (120 meters) high. So at the same moment, the lake was going down, the ground was sinking, and air was shooting upward in fountains.

The lake's own fresh water had gone into the mine. Its place was now taken by salt water coming from the Delcambre Canal and Vermilion Bay. Our sources do not give a minute-by-minute account of how fast all this happened. We only know it took several hours.

And did you know that some of the barges pulled into the whirlpool later came back to the surface? We will return to that at the end. One more thing: no human life was lost in all this chaos. But the question is, how did the 55 people inside the mine get out?

chapters.covers: Electrician noticed torrent and sounded alarm; orderly escape via only elevator; six employees awarded for heroism; rig crew of seven fled; fisherman reached shore; no human deaths, three dogs killed.

articleEn: How did the 55 people inside the mine survive? The answer begins with an ordinary moment, when someone noticed water. The electrician at the Diamond Crystal mine was the one who saw a torrent of water. Instead of staying quiet, he sounded the alarm immediately. According to our sources, that alarm alerted everyone. It was only thanks to the electrician's timely warning that people were able to leave the mine.

The mine had several levels reaching down 1,500 feet, and there was only one elevator to get out from that depth. Fifty-five people, one elevator, and rising water. Yet the sources say there was no panic. People used the elevator in an orderly way. The reason, according to the sources, was the employees' discipline and training. What they had learned came in useful at exactly the right moment. This matters because the mine's tunnels were huge, each about 100 by 80 feet. When the water began dissolving the salt pillars, the tunnels started to fall in. In such conditions every minute counted, yet people kept leaving in an orderly manner. In the end, all 55 employees got out of the mine. Not one person was left behind. Later, Diamond Crystal gave awards to six employees for their bravery.

Now let's go to the surface. On the drilling rig above the lake, there was a crew of seven. They too were in a place that was about to change. The crew left the platform just before the rig fell, and the platform then dropped into the lake's new depths. Think about it: what if they had stayed a few moments longer? The sources do not answer that question. We only know that all seven got out in time.

There was one more person on the lake. A fisherman was out in his small boat. When the commotion began, he got his boat to the shore, and so he too stayed safe. His name is not recorded in the sources. He was an unnamed man who got his boat out just in time.

Now the most important point: no human life was lost in this entire accident. That may bring some relief, since the scene looked extremely dangerous. According to the sources, however, three dogs died, which was a sad part of that day. But the survival of every person was truly extraordinary. Look at the numbers: 55 people in the mine, 7 on the rig, and one fisherman on the lake. At least 63 people were there, and all of them survived.

So was it just luck? Perhaps partly. But the sources are clear that the electrician's alertness and the employees' training played a major role. Still, one question remained: who was responsible for this destruction? Was the drilling done in the wrong place, or were the mine's maps wrong?

articleEn: Now for the hardest question: who was to blame for the disaster? The answer is not easy, because the very thing that could have proven the truth was washed away in the whirlpool. According to the sources, the evidence that could have confirmed the root cause was swept away. Investigators had little left to examine at the scene.

Even so, the work did not stop. Engineers from Texaco and Diamond Crystal worked together after the accident to find the likely location of the hole. They estimated that it was probably in the mine's 1,300-foot level, in a section where salt had already been removed. Remember that the rig's 14-inch drill assembly had become stuck that morning at 1,228 feet, and that the rig began to tilt about two and a half hours later. Was the sticking a sign of some mistake? The sources reach no conclusion on this, and we will not turn guesses into facts.

So what was the official outcome? The Mine Safety and Health Administration, or MSHA, investigated the accident but could not assign responsibility. The reason was simple. MSHA could not determine whether Texaco had been drilling in the wrong place or whether the mine's maps were inaccurate. Only two possibilities were on the table: either the rig's location was wrongly chosen, or the mine's maps did not match reality. Proving either one required solid evidence, but the evidence had already been washed away. That is why a decision was not possible.

MSHA issued its report on the incident in August 1981. It described what happened, but it gave no official cause. Doesn't that seem strange? Such a huge accident, and even the official report offers no clear reason. That is what keeps the story interesting to this day.

There is one more fact. The rig was doing exploratory drilling along the edge of the salt dome, and the salt mine lay right beneath the lake. Was any company officially held responsible? No. But the matter did not end there, because compensation settlements came later, which we will cover shortly.

One more point: none of our sources blames any single individual, and we will not accuse anyone without proof. The matter still deserves attention. When there is a mine underground and drilling above, this accident showed how large the consequences can be.

articleEn: Now for what we left for later. A few days afterward, once the pressure equalized, 9 of the 11 barges came back up to the surface of the lake. The lake itself had changed too. The freshwater lake that was once 10 feet deep was now filled with salty water from the Delcambre Canal and Vermilion Bay. And its depth? Today Lake Peigneur's maximum depth is 200 feet, making it the deepest lake in Louisiana. From 10 feet to 200 feet!

Now the cost. In 1983, Texaco and the drilling contractor Wilson Brothers paid Diamond Crystal 32 million dollars in an out-of-court settlement. Another settlement followed: Texaco, Wilson Brothers and Diamond Crystal together paid a total of 12.8 million dollars to Live Oak Gardens, the botanical garden and plant nursery. So the damage was not limited to the mine; a botanical garden was affected as well. These sums were meant to make up for the losses.

What became of the mine? Diamond Crystal's mine, which had been running since 1919, was closed in December 1986, ending a long journey. But the story of the dome did not end. Since 1994, AGL Resources has used the salt dome beneath the lake for storing pressurized natural gas and as a gas hub. In 2009, local residents voiced concern, asking how safe it was to store gas under the lake while drilling continued nearby.

So what do we learn from this whole story? The first lesson is about training. The 55 people who used the elevator in an orderly way all survived. The second lesson is about maps and communication, because in the end nobody could determine where the mistake occurred. That question may stay open forever.

Friends, what do you think was the real cause? Drilling in the wrong place, or the mine's inaccurate maps? Do write your opinion in the comments. If you liked this video, please like it, share it with people you know, and don't forget to subscribe to the channel. See you in the next story.

shorts.text: ایک پوری جھیل چند گھنٹوں میں غائب ہو گئی، کیا آپ یقین کریں گے؟ 20 November 1980 کی صبح Louisiana کی Lake Peigneur ایک بہت بڑے whirlpool میں بدل گئی۔ اس whirlpool نے drilling platform کو نگل لیا۔ ساتھ میں 11 barges، ایک tugboat اور بہت سے درخت بھی غائب ہو گئے۔ تقریباً 65 acres زمین، جس میں Jefferson Island کا بڑا حصہ بھی تھا، ایک sinkhole میں سما گئی۔ پھر ایک اور عجیب بات ہوئی۔ Delcambre Canal، جو عام طور پر جھیل کا پانی Vermilion Bay میں لے جاتی ہے، الٹی سمت میں بہنے لگی۔ نمکین پانی خالی جھیل کی طرف دوڑا، اور چند دن کے لیے Louisiana کا سب سے اونچا waterfall بن گیا۔ اس کی اونچائی 164 فٹ تھی۔ مگر جھیل کے نیچے آخر ایسا کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek poori jheel chand ghanton mein ghayab ho gayi, kya aap yaqeen karenge? 20 November 1980 ki subah Louisiana ki Lake Peigneur ek bohat bare whirlpool mein badal gayi. Is whirlpool ne drilling platform ko nigal liya. Sath mein 11 barges, ek tugboat aur bohat se darakht bhi ghayab ho gaye. Taqreeban 65 acres zameen, jis mein Jefferson Island ka bara hissa bhi tha, ek sinkhole mein sama gayi. Phir ek aur ajeeb baat hui. Delcambre Canal, jo aam tor par jheel ka pani Vermilion Bay mein le jati hai, ulti simt mein behne lagi. Namkeen pani khali jheel ki taraf dora, aur chand din ke liye Louisiana ka sab se ooncha waterfall ban gaya. Is ki oonchai 164 fut thi. Magar jheel ke neeche aakhir aisa kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 20 November 1980, a Louisiana lake drained into a salt mine beneath it.
The canal even flowed backwards and created a 164-foot waterfall.

shorts.text: 55 لوگ، صرف ایک elevator، اور بڑھتا ہوا پانی۔ وہ بچے کیسے؟ 20 November 1980 کو Diamond Crystal کی salt mine کے electrician نے پانی کی تیز دھار یعنی torrent دیکھی۔ اس نے خاموش رہنے کے بجائے فوراً alarm بجا دیا۔ mine کی کئی levels تھیں اور وہ 1,500 فٹ گہرائی تک جاتی تھیں۔ باہر نکلنے کے لیے صرف ایک elevator تھی۔ مگر وہاں افراتفری نہیں مچی۔ employees کے discipline اور training کی وجہ سے سب نے منظم طریقے سے elevator کے ذریعے نکلنا شروع کیا۔ تمام 55 employees محفوظ نکل آئے، اور 6 کو Diamond Crystal نے ان کی بہادری پر awards دیے۔ اوپر جھیل پر drilling rig کا 7 افراد کا crew بھی platform چھوڑ چکا تھا۔ مگر ان کے پیچھے کیا ہونے والا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 55 log, sirf ek elevator, aur barhta hua pani. Woh bache kaise? 20 November 1980 ko Diamond Crystal ki salt mine ke electrician ne pani ki tez dhaar yani torrent dekhi. Is ne khamosh rehne ke bajaye fauran alarm baja diya. Mine ki kai levels thin aur woh 1,500 fut gehrai tak jati thin. Bahar nikalne ke liye sirf ek elevator thi. Magar wahan afratafri nahi machi. Employees ke discipline aur training ki wajah se sab ne munazzam tareeqe se elevator ke zariye nikalna shuru kiya. Tamam 55 employees mehfooz nikal aaye, aur 6 ko Diamond Crystal ne un ki bahaduri par awards diye. Upar jheel par drilling rig ka 7 afrad ka crew bhi platform chhor chuka tha. Magar un ke peechhe kya hone wala tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

All 55 employees escaped a flooding salt mine through its only elevator.
An electrician's quick alarm and the crew's training made the difference.

shorts.text: ایک تباہی، اور اس کا ثبوت خود بھنور میں بہہ گیا! قصوروار کون تھا؟ Sources کے مطابق جو شواہد اصل وجہ بتا سکتے تھے، وہ whirlpool میں بہہ گئے۔ اس صبح rig کا 14 inch کا drill assembly 1,228 فٹ پر پھنس گیا تھا، اور ڈھائی گھنٹے بعد rig ٹیڑھی ہونے لگی۔ پھر drill assembly نے mine کو چھید دیا اور میٹھا پانی نمک کو گھلاتا گیا۔ Texaco اور Diamond Crystal کے engineers نے بعد میں مل کر کام کیا۔ ان کا اندازہ تھا کہ سوراخ mine کی 1,300 فٹ والی level کے اس حصے میں تھا جہاں سے نمک نکالا جا چکا تھا۔ Mine Safety and Health Administration کسی کو ذمہ دار نہ ٹھہرا سکی، کیونکہ وہ طے نہ کر سکی کہ Texaco غلط جگہ drill کر رہی تھی یا mine کے نقشے غلط تھے۔ تو سچ کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek tabahi, aur is ka saboot khud bhanwar mein beh gaya! Qasoorwar kaun tha? Sources ke mutabiq jo shawahid asal wajah bata sakte thay, woh whirlpool mein beh gaye. Is subah rig ka 14 inch ka drill assembly 1,228 fut par phans gaya tha, aur dhai ghante baad rig terhi hone lagi. Phir drill assembly ne mine ko chheed diya aur meetha pani namak ko gholta gaya. Texaco aur Diamond Crystal ke engineers ne baad mein mil kar kaam kiya. Un ka andaza tha ke surakh mine ki 1,300 fut wali level ke us hisse mein tha jahan se namak nikala ja chuka tha. Mine Safety and Health Administration kisi ko zimmedar na thehra saki, kyunke woh tay na kar saki ke Texaco ghalat jagah drill kar rahi thi ya mine ke naqshe ghalat thay. To sach kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

The evidence was washed away, and investigators could not assign blame.
